body: The air conditioner hums at a pitch that gets into the microphones, so at ten past seven on a Sunday morning a young man in a room above a hardware shop is switching it off. The room is immediately too hot. Four singers arrange themselves around one condenser mic that has been repaired twice and is held at the base with tape. The song they are tracking was written on Thursday, has been sung in public exactly twice, and will be on somebody’s phone in another country by Wednesday. Nobody in that room thinks of this as a mission project. They think of it as work, and they are behind on it.
That room is a broadcaster. Almost nothing about the way Christian media is organised is arranged to notice that, and the vocabulary is where the failure shows up most plainly.

Almost all Christian broadcasting still runs on a nineteenth-century map. Content is made in a handful of wealthy countries and sent outward; the receiving end is described as a field, and the traffic is understood to move in one direction only.

Take the word field literally, because it is doing far more work than the people using it realise. A field is worked. It is cleared, sown, watered and harvested, and every one of those verbs has the same subject, and the subject is not the field. A field does not commission anything. It does not decide what it needs, it does not judge the quality of what lands on it, and it cannot send anything back. Reaching, going, sending — the vocabulary is perfectly consistent, and every word of it positions the listener as a destination rather than as a participant. Nobody using those words means any harm by them. That is precisely why they have survived: they sound like devotion, and they carry an assumption nobody has looked at directly in about a century.

This dial carries 121 stations between HM 300.30 and HM 398.70, and every one of them holds a number that cannot be reassigned to anything else later. Four of those numbers are African and not one of them is playing tonight: HM 329.30 Africa Inspire (Kiswahili), HM 330.90 West Africa Inspire (Yorùbá), HM 331.50 Ethiopia Inspire (አማርኛ) and HM 355.60 Jubilee Prayers in Swahili are assigned, held, and still in build.

Those numbers were committed before there was a second of audio to put on them, which is the expensive way round and the honest one. A frequency held open is a frequency that cannot be handed to something more popular in six months. It is a public promise with a date on it that nobody controls. The reason for doing it in that order is not complicated: the centre of gravity of the Church moved decades ago. Most of the media has not been told. Building the numbers first is one way of admitting the map was wrong before the schedule has caught up with the admission.

You can see the old map most clearly in the pictures. The appeal photograph is a child, the caption is a need, and the implied relationship runs downhill. It is not that the need is imaginary, or that generosity is a bad thing. It is that a century of that framing has trained an entire industry to expect nothing back, and an industry that expects nothing back will never go looking for a host, a catalogue, or an editorial judgement seated in a place it has only ever sent parcels to. At that point it has stopped being condescension and become plain incuriosity, which is harder to argue with and does more damage.

So the band is partitioned by language rather than by target. The multilanguage block runs its own stretch of the dial, with the praise and worship frequencies grouped together and a prayer block sitting further up it, each number held in a single tongue with a host inside it. Learn roughly where the block sits and you can move about in it without reading anything, which is exactly the skill a real dial teaches and a search box never can.
The alternative is not wicked. It is simply cheaper, it is what almost everybody does, and it is called dubbing.

Be fair to translation first, because it is honourable work and the whole faith depends on it. The Scriptures are translated. Hymns have crossed languages for centuries and gained things in the crossing. Subtitles have carried teaching into places no broadcaster could have reached on its own. But a dubbed station is a fundamentally different object from a hosted one. It has no repertoire of its own, because everything on it was selected somewhere else and then rendered. It has no editorial judgement seated in the culture, so nobody anywhere in the chain is in a position to say that a song is embarrassing, or dated, or exactly right for this particular month. What comes out is accurate and inert, and listeners can tell inside a minute.
A field receives. A broadcaster decides.

A man of sixty is sitting in a hospital car park in Yorkshire with forty minutes to go before visiting hours and no wish at all to go in early. He leaves the radio on whatever it happened to land on. What comes out is a language he does not know, sung by a choir that is plainly not being paid, over an organ and a drum, and it goes on and on — well past the point at which an English song would have stopped and explained itself. He understands not one word of it. He sits through all of it with both hands on the wheel. When he does go in he is steadier than he was, and if anybody asked him why he would say something about the singing and then give up.

That is the traffic running the other way, and it is not a special case or a happy accident. It is what happens whenever material made properly for its own audience is allowed to be overheard by somebody it was not made for.

The cost of saying all this now is obvious and there is no way round it. Four African frequencies are assigned on this dial and not one of them plays a note tonight. A number with no audio on it is a promise rather than a programme, and anybody at all can print a promise. If you came to this article expecting to put Yorùbá praise on in the car this afternoon, you cannot, and no amount of argument about maps and vocabulary alters that.

But notice what the silence is evidence of. A mission field gets programming when there happens to be programming to give it, and it never gets a number, because a number is a commitment made in advance and commitments of that kind are not made to fields. Assigning the frequency first, publishing it where anybody can see it, and then having to answer for the silence is what a broadcaster does. The awkwardness is the proof. It would have been much easier to say nothing at all until the audio existed, and considerably less honest.

So the claim is narrow and it is not a slogan. Africa is not a category on this dial and it is not a destination for other people’s output. It is a set of held frequencies with hosts attached, sitting inside the same numbering scheme as everything else, subject to the same standards and answerable to the same audiences. Material made for a field is made down. Material made for an audience is made properly, because the people making it expect to be judged by them.
All of which stays theoretical unless you can hear the model working somewhere tonight. You can.

The international part of the band is the largest thing on it: 40 stations across 29 languages, each one hosted in its own tongue rather than translated into it afterwards, with a catalogue chosen by somebody who lives inside the culture and fully expects to be told when they have got it wrong. Some of those frequencies are on air tonight and some are still being built. The ones that are on air are the argument in audible form, and they are not there to demonstrate anything to anybody. They are simply stations, which is the entire point being made.

If you want the shortest route to hearing it, go to HM 328.70 — Inspire Crown (العربية), which is on air now. Arabic is as much an African language as a Middle Eastern one, and the station carries Coptic music alongside Maronite and Levantine material: the Coptic tradition is Egyptian, it is African, and it is older than most of the institutions that later drew the maps this article has been complaining about. What you get is praise hosted in the language rather than a Western catalogue with new words fitted over the top, and you will hear the difference within a minute even if you do not have a syllable of Arabic. Listen to how long the phrases are, and to what the singers do with the ends of lines.

There is nothing to install and nothing to buy. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays; the whole thing is built for inexpensive handsets and thin connections, which is not a courtesy but a design requirement for a band with this much of the world on it. Add the page to your home screen if you want it closer to hand and it opens like anything else on there. And do make yourself an account while you are on it — it is free, it carries your favourites across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for. That is how the queue for the silent ones gets ordered.

So treat this as an invitation rather than a demonstration. Put it on this afternoon while you are doing something else, and let it run well past the point where you would ordinarily have changed it. You are not evaluating a culture and you are not supporting a cause; both of those are the old map wearing a newer coat. You are listening to a station that was made properly by people who assumed somebody like you might one day be listening — which is what broadcasting is, and which is the only relationship worth having with a continent that has been talked about for quite long enough.
